name: Sales and business development
summary: Sales and business development interviews usually test whether you can sell, not just talk about selling: expect questions on your targets and how you met them, how you handle objections and rejection, and often a role-play where you pitch a product or deal with a tough customer. For experienced roles, interviewers commonly dig into your pipeline, your numbers and the deals you won or lost.
rounds: Recruiter or HR screen on your background, targets and expectations
Interview with the hiring or sales manager on your track record and how you sell
Role-play for many roles: a cold call, a product pitch or handling an objection
For senior roles, often a presentation such as a territory or account plan
Final round with a senior leader or HR
looks_for: Results you can state clearly: the target, what you achieved and how
Listening and asking questions before pitching
Bouncing back from rejection and keeping up a steady routine of follow-ups
Pipeline discipline: tracking leads, stages and next steps
Integrity: not overpromising to close a deal

questions.text: Tell me about a deal you're proud of closing. How did it come together?
covers: The customer, what they needed and who made the decision
The steps from first contact to close, including one setback
Your own part in it and the result

questions.text: Tell me about a month or quarter when you missed your target. What happened?
covers: The size of the gap, stated honestly
What caused it and which parts were in your control
What you changed and how the next period went

questions.text: Describe a deal you lost that you expected to win.
covers: Why you thought it was going well
What you later learned about why they chose someone else
How it changed the way you qualify or follow up

questions.text: Tell me about a time you turned an unhappy customer into a repeat buyer.
covers: What went wrong for them and how you found out
What you did to fix it, including help from other teams
The business that came back and why

questions.text: Tell me about a time you needed operations, finance or delivery to help you keep a promise to a customer.
covers: What you had promised and why it needed their help
How you asked, and what you offered them in return
Whether the customer got what they were promised

questions.text: Pick something on the desk, or your phone, and sell it to me in two minutes.
covers: Asking one or two questions about my needs before pitching
Benefits linked to what I told you, not a list of features
A clear ask or next step at the end

questions.text: A prospect says, 'Your price is too high.' How would you respond?
covers: Finding out what they're comparing it with
Restating the value in terms of their problem
Knowing when a smaller package, better terms or walking away is right

questions.text: How would you qualify a lead? What tells you it's worth your time?
covers: Need, budget, who decides and timing, or a similar checklist
The questions you'd ask on the first call
When you'd stop chasing a lead

questions.text: Walk me through how you'd open a cold call to a business that has never heard of us.
covers: A short, specific reason for calling them in particular
A question that gets them talking about their problem
A small next step to ask for, such as a meeting or a demo

questions.text: How do you plan a week of prospecting and follow-ups?
covers: Blocking time for new outreach, follow-ups and meetings
Prioritising by deal size and how close each lead is to buying
Tracking activity so you can see what actually turns into sales

questions.text: A large customer goes silent after a promising meeting. What would you do?
covers: Following up with something useful, not just 'checking in'
Trying another contact in the company carefully
Deciding when to step back and how you'd keep the door open

questions.text: Which numbers would you track to know whether your pipeline is healthy?
covers: Leads at each stage, conversion between stages, average deal size and sales cycle length
Pipeline value compared with your target
What you'd do if one stage is weak

questions.text: How would you start selling in a new city or industry where we have no customers yet?
covers: Researching who buys, why and who they buy from today
A first list of target accounts and a way in, such as referrals or events
Early signs you'd watch to know whether it's working

questions.text: How have you used a CRM, and what do you record after a sales call?
covers: The tool you used and how often you updated it
What you record: needs, objections, decision-makers, next step and date
How good records helped you or a colleague close a deal

questions.text: Tell me about yourself in a way that would make me want to keep listening.
covers: A short, confident opening about who you are
One result or experience that shows you can sell
Why this role is the next step for you

questions.text: Why sales? What do you enjoy about it, and what do you find hardest?
covers: What draws you to selling, shown by something you've done
An honest hard part, such as rejection or long sales cycles
How you deal with that hard part

questions.text: This role has targets and part of the pay depends on results. How would you handle a slow month?
covers: Comfort with targets and incentive-based pay, stated honestly
What you'd do differently in a slow month: more outreach, better leads, asking for help
How you keep your energy up when results lag

tips: Know your numbers well: targets, achievement, deal sizes and conversion rates. Interviewers commonly ask for them and follow up.
In a role-play, ask two or three questions before you pitch; jumping straight to features is an easy mistake to avoid.
Freshers: college fest sponsorships, part-time jobs, internships or a small business of your own all make good sales stories.
Talk about what you do when a customer says no, not only when they say yes.
Never claim a number you can't explain; a follow-up question will usually expose it.
Learn the company's product and customers well enough to pitch it in one minute if asked.
